summary: ARINC 835-2, an information report published in December 2025, gives guidance on securing loadable software parts used in aircraft systems with digital signatures and public key infrastructure (PKI), to ensure their integrity and authenticity. summary: In the AUTOSAR Secure Hardware Extensions (SHE) specification, the secure-boot command has SHE verify the MAC of the bootloader. The Uptane Standard 2.1.0, a framework for securing ground vehicle software update systems, gives RSA and ECDSA as examples of the public key cryptographic algorithm used by the key, and rsassa-pss-sha256 and ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 as examples of the scheme used to verify the signature. The FuSeCar project deliverable D3.1 states that conventional digital signature schemes based on RSA and ECC are vulnerable to quantum attacks, as Shor's algorithm could break them on sufficiently powerful quantum computers. The NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ says NSA wants the transition for firmware roots of trust, which it expects for some long-lived signatures, to begin now using LMS and XMSS whenever possible rather than waiting for ML-DSA. The same FAQ says validated ML-DSA is approved for all signing use cases and may be the most appropriate choice for some software and firmware signing use cases. NIST SP 800-208 says that stateful hash-based signature schemes are primarily intended for applications that need a digital signature scheme in the near future, whose implementation will have a long lifetime, and for which it would not be practical to transition to a different digital signature scheme once deployed, and that the authentication of firmware updates for constrained devices is an application that may fit this profile. The FuSeCar project deliverable D3.1 considers CRYSTALS-Dilithium and Falcon as the post-quantum digital signature algorithms to evaluate for authenticity in automotive over-the-air software updates. ISO's catalogue page for ISO/SAE 21434:2021, Road vehicles - Cybersecurity engineering, says the standard applies to the entire lifecycle of electrical and electronic (E/E) systems in vehicles, from concept and development to production, operation, maintenance and decommissioning.
main_source: ISO/SAE 21434 Road Vehicle Cybersecurity

summary: AUTOSAR's TCP/IP Stack specification (R25-11) requires that, where TLS ciphersuites include support for elliptic curves, at least the corresponding key exchange algorithms according to section 2 of RFC 4492, such as ECDHE, be implemented. AUTOSAR's Security Overview (R25-11) describes MACsec key management as starting from a pre-shared key (CAK): a unique, cryptographically strong random key that is pre-configured and securely stored on each ECU involved in the communication. AUTOSAR's Security Overview (R25-11) lists as a disadvantage of (D)TLS that the current TLS standards do not yet provide post-quantum-ready asymmetric cryptography. AUTOSAR's Secure Onboard Communication (SecOC) specification (R25-11) is based on the assumption that mainly symmetric authentication approaches with message authentication codes (MACs) are used. AUTOSAR's Security Overview (R25-11) states that all asymmetric cryptographic algorithms required or recommended by the AUTOSAR standard can be compromised once quantum computers are advanced enough to apply Shor's algorithm to the keys in use. AUTOSAR's Security Overview (R25-11) also says that symmetric cryptography like AES is less severely impacted by quantum computers, as no quantum algorithm is currently known to be able to break it. AUTOSAR's Security Overview (R25-11) lists secure storage of sensitive data such as cryptographic keys and certificates among the typical features of an automotive Hardware Security Module. UN Regulation No. 155 (paragraph 7.3.8) requires that cryptographic modules used for the purpose of the Regulation be in line with consensus standards and, where they are not, that the vehicle manufacturer justify their use.
main_source: ISO/SAE 21434 Road Vehicle Cybersecurity

summary: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 says SCADA systems are used to monitor and control oil and natural gas distribution, including pipelines. RFC 7296, which describes version 2 of the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) protocol, states that IKE is a component of IPsec used for performing mutual authentication and establishing and maintaining Security Associations (SAs). RFC 8784, an Internet Standards Track document, describes an extension of IKEv2 to allow it to be resistant to a quantum computer by using preshared keys. RFC 9370 describes how to extend IKEv2 to allow multiple key exchanges to take place while computing a shared secret during a Security Association (SA) setup. RFC 9370 allows the negotiation of one or more post-quantum algorithms to exchange data in addition to the existing (EC)DH key exchange data. summary: ETSI TS 119 312 V2.1.1 (June 2026) lists cryptographic suites used for the creation and validation of digital signatures, electronic timestamps, electronic registered delivery services, electronic archiving, electronic ledgers and related certificates. It says it incorporates requirements for the transition to post-quantum cryptography, including hybrid cryptographic schemes and the phasing out of legacy mechanisms. It says that where protection against attacks leveraging quantum computers is required, for example where the long-term validity of a signature extends beyond 2030, RSA shall be used in a hybrid scheme or replaced by a quantum-safe algorithm. It says that ML-DSA as specified in NIST FIPS 204 shall be used as a recommended mechanism. It says that SLH-DSA as specified in NIST FIPS 205 shall be used as a recommended mechanism. It says that LMS as specified in IETF RFC 8554 and XMSS as specified in IETF RFC 8391 shall be used as recommended mechanisms, subject to the condition specified in its note. It adds that the use of LMS and XMSS is therefore restricted to deployment environments where state management can be strictly enforced. Annex A of the document sets requirements for the hash function and the signature algorithm used in CAdES and PAdES signatures.

summary: Safe (formerly Gnosis Safe), the dominant DeFi multisig standard, enforces an M-of-N owner threshold on-chain: checkNSignatures() requires signatures from at least the configured threshold of owners, each verified independently via ecrecover (ECDSA/secp256k1), with owner addresses checked in strict ascending order to prevent duplicates. This is a plain multisig — N independent classical signatures checked against a count — not a cryptographic threshold-signature scheme (no MPC key-splitting). Safe also accepts EIP-1271 contract signatures and, more recently, secp256r1 (passkey) signatures via the RIP-7212 precompile, but the underlying primitive for owner keys remains classical ECDSA.

summary: TNO, NXP and InfIoT upgraded OCPP with hybrid quantum-safe cryptography (TLS handshake and X.509 certificates) for electric vehicle charging infrastructure, as described in a talk abstract at the PKI Consortium PQC Conference 2025 (Kuala Lumpur); the protocol was tested on an NXP i.MX 8 board similar to those in real charging stations and, per the abstract, will be used in the EnergyPod.

use_case_label: Distributed energy resources & EV charging (IEEE 2030.5 / OCPP)
summary: Per a 2022 Sandia report, IEEE 2030.5 distributed-energy-resource communications require TLS 1.2 with ECDHE_ECDSA and X.509v3 certificates, and a SunSpec/Sandia workgroup recommends requiring at least TLS 1.2 and recommends TLS 1.3 for all DER communications. For EV charging, a conference talk abstract reports that TNO, NXP and InfinIoT upgraded OCPP with hybrid quantum-safe cryptography (TLS handshake and X.509 certificates), tested on an NXP i.MX 8 board and intended for use in the EnergyPod; the abstract names no algorithm.
main_source: Distributed Energy Resource Cybersecurity Standards Development - Final Project Report (SAND2022-1118)

summary: BIP-360 proposes, via a soft fork, a Pay-to-Merkle-Root (P2MR) output type that works like Taproot (P2TR) outputs with the key path spend removed. The BIP has Draft status, and Taproot is the only currently activated output type that supports script trees. P2MR does not by itself protect against short exposure quantum attacks; the BIP's authors say they intend to offer a separate proposal for post-quantum signatures upon further research.
main_source: Bitcoin BIP-360: Pay-to-Merkle-Root (P2MR)
no_protocol_reason: Bitcoin output types are chain-specific consensus rules (a soft-fork proposal), not a standardised network protocol tracked by the matrix.

summary: Australia's New Payments Platform (NPP) is the country's real-time retail payment infrastructure; it uses ISO 20022 pacs.008 messages and processes over 5.2 million transactions daily under a 2,000 millisecond end-to-end service level. A 2026 simulation study (an arXiv preprint, not a deployment) modelled the post-quantum signature algorithms ML-DSA, SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) and Falcon on this platform: under its modelled parameters all ML-DSA and Falcon variants met the service level, while SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) was disqualified by queue saturation.
main_source: Post-Quantum Cryptography Migration in Australian Real-Time Payment Infrastructure: A Monte Carlo Simulation Study of the New Payments Platform
no_protocol_reason: NPP is a national real-time platform whose payments are ISO 20022 pacs.008 messages routed through a central NPPA hub, not a standardised network protocol.

use_case_label: Open banking access interfaces and provider certificates (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389)
summary: Under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389, which sets regulatory technical standards for strong customer authentication and common and secure open standards of communication, payment service providers must rely on qualified certificates for electronic seals or for website authentication to identify themselves to account-servicing providers, and must apply secure encryption using strong and widely recognised encryption techniques to data exchanged over the internet.
main_source: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389 — RTS on Strong Customer Authentication and Common and Secure Communication
no_protocol_reason: The regulation requires identification with qualified certificates and secure encryption between the parties but names no specific protocol.

use_case_label: Federal civilian high-value assets and high impact systems (EO 14412 / OMB M-26-15)
summary: Executive Order 14412 (22 June 2026) directs OMB guidance requiring agencies to review their inventories of high value assets (HVAs) and high impact systems, excluding national security systems, and to transition all HVAs and high impact systems to post-quantum cryptography for key establishment by 31 December 2030 and for digital signatures by 31 December 2031. OMB memorandum M-26-15 (24 June 2026) implements the order for agencies: each must submit a PQC migration plan within 120 days, in phases from strategy and discovery (2026-2027) through pilots and early migration (2027-2028), prioritized migration of key establishment (2028-2030) and signature migration (2031) to full migration (2035). GSA is to set up an inter-agency working group on federal identity, credential and access management (FICAM) to support PQC within 60 days. The memorandum does not apply to national security systems.
main_source: OMB Memorandum M-26-15 — Execution of the Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography
no_protocol_reason: Federal PQC migration is directed by policy and a phased schedule across agency systems, not by a single wire protocol.

summary: PIV card credentials use RSA or ECDSA signature keys and RSA key-transport or ECDH key-management keys (NIST SP 800-78-5, July 2024). On 12 June 2026 NIST released initial working drafts of proposed updates to SP 800-73 (Parts 1 and 2) and SP 800-78 to support post-quantum cryptography in PIV; the drafts identify the changes expected to be needed to use ML-DSA and ML-KEM. The approach under consideration is a dual-stack model that preserves existing classical PIV keys and data objects and adds new key references, certificate containers and data objects for PQC credentials. NIST describes these as preliminary working materials, not formal public drafts.
main_source: NIST SP 800-78-6 (Initial Working Draft), Cryptographic Algorithms and Key Sizes for Personal Identity Verification

summary: NIAP Policy Letter #33 (31 August 2026, effective 1 January 2027) sets the timeline for post-quantum requirements in Common Criteria evaluations: placement on the NIAP Product Compliant List (PCL) makes a product eligible for procurement for use in national security systems. Products that do not meet CNSA 1.0 minimum requirements for every cryptographic function will not be accepted into evaluation from 1 January 2027 and will not be posted to the PCL from 1 July 2027; products that do not meet CNSA 2.0 requirements for every cryptographic function will not be accepted into evaluation from 1 January 2028 and will not be posted to the PCL from 1 January 2029. Products meeting all CNSA 2.0 requirements are prioritized for validation resources. NSA's draft CSfC PQC guidance addendum (version 1.0 draft .5, April 2025) gives a currently planned CSfC timeline, subject to change, aiming for all CSfC solutions to implement post-quantum cryptography by 2030.
main_source: NIAP CCEVS Policy Letter 33 — Post Quantum Cryptography Implementation
no_protocol_reason: NIAP Policy #33 sets evaluation and listing deadlines for products, not a wire protocol.
certification_future: NIAP Policy #33 (effective 1 January 2027): products that do not meet CNSA 1.0 minimum requirements for every cryptographic function are not accepted into evaluation from 1 January 2027 and not posted to the PCL from 1 July 2027; products that do not meet CNSA 2.0 requirements for every cryptographic function are not accepted into evaluation from 1 January 2028 and not posted to the PCL from 1 January 2029.

use_case_label: Defense industrial base and federal contractors
summary: Executive Order 14412 (22 June 2026) directs the Federal Acquisition Regulatory Council to publish, within 180 days of the order, a proposed rule amending the Federal Acquisition Regulation to require covered contractors to comply by 31 December 2030 with NIST's FIPS, including all applicable FIPS incorporating PQC-compliant algorithms. The order directs a proposed rule; it is not itself that rule.
main_source: Executive Order 14412 (June 22, 2026): Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks

use_case_label: Entropy sources for random bit generation
summary: NIST SP 800-90B specifies the design principles and requirements for the entropy sources used by random bit generators, and the tests for validating them. FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance covers a hardware module with an entropy-generating source inside its cryptographic boundary, and notes that ML-KEM encapsulation requires randomness.
main_source: SP 800-90B: Recommendation for the Entropy Sources Used for Random Bit Generation
no_protocol_reason: Entropy-source validation is a module-level requirement, not a protocol tracked by the matrix.

summary: Each Matter device holds a number of certificate chains. Its device attestation certificate (DAC) proves the authenticity of the manufacturer and is used by the commissioner during commissioning. The attestation chapter refers to ECDSA with SHA-256 on the elliptic curve secp256r1 (NIST P-256). A note in the Matter 1.6 text says that PQC Phase 1 will likely soon replace the AttestationCryptoInfo mechanism in the onboarding payload with an equivalent mechanism using the Operational Credentials cluster.
main_source: Matter 1.6 Core Specification
vetting_body: Connectivity Standards Alliance (CSA) Board of Directors
no_protocol_reason: Matter commissioning attestation is a smart-home consortium specification, not a protocol tracked by the matrix.

use_case_label: Content provenance and authenticity (C2PA Content Credentials)
summary: The C2PA Technical Specification 2.4 requires digital signatures to use its allowed list: ECDSA (ES256, ES384, ES512), RSASSA-PSS (PS256, PS384, PS512) and EdDSA (Ed25519 only). The deprecated list is empty.
main_source: Content Credentials: C2PA Technical Specification, Version 2.4
no_protocol_reason: C2PA Content Credentials is a media-provenance manifest format, not a protocol tracked by the matrix.

summary: Network tokenization replaces the card number (PAN) with a token that is exchanged back for the PAN held in a token vault; EMV 3-D Secure core components (ACS, DS and 3DS server) fall under the PCI 3DS Core Security Standard, which requires strong cryptography for 3DS data in transit and a trusted certificate authority for 3DS digital certificates.
main_source: PCI 3DS Core Security Standard v1.0 — ROC Reporting Template
no_protocol_reason: EMV 3-D Secure and network tokenization are payment-scheme specifications, not network protocols tracked by the matrix.

summary: 5G roaming signalling crosses the N32 interface between security edge protection proxies (SEPPs): directly over TLS on N32-c, or through PRINS (JOSE message protection) when an IPX provider is in the path. ATIS analyses SEPP-to-SEPP communications as exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later. ATIS says the following upgrades are necessary for SEPP-to-SEPP communications to maintain robust security against future quantum threats: mTLS 1.3 with PQC-compliant crypto-suites (e.g. ML-KEM) for key establishment, and PKI certificates with PQC-compliant digital signature algorithms (e.g. ML-DSA).
main_source: ATIS — Preparing 5G for the Quantum Era: An Analysis of 3GPP Architecture and the Transition to Quantum-Resistant Cryptography

summary: Microchip's April 2026 release introduces the TS1800 platform root-of-trust controller and the TS50x secure-boot controller, with hardware accelerators for the NIST-standardised ML-DSA, LMS verification and ML-KEM; the TS50x verifies firmware signatures in a hybrid of classical ECC P-384 and PQC. Both are available through an early-adopter program. Vendor-stated; not independently cross-checked.
main_source: Microchip Expands Family of Post-Quantum-Ready Root of Trust Controllers
no_protocol_reason: A platform root-of-trust / secure-boot controller IC (secure boot, firmware update, attestation), not a network protocol tracked by the Algorithms > Protocol Support matrix.

use_case_label: Secure messaging (Signal PQXDH and SPQR, iMessage PQ3, MLS)
summary: Signal's October 2025 post announces the Sparse Post Quantum Ratchet (SPQR), a further step after its PQXDH upgrade, which it mixes with its existing double ratchet as a triple ratchet, and says Signal is rolling it out slowly and carefully; Signal's PQXDH specification notes that it still relies on the hardness of the discrete log problem for mutual authentication. Apple's February 2024 post says Signal added support for the PQXDH protocol and that support for PQ3, iMessage's post-quantum protocol, will start to roll out with iOS 17.4 and the matching releases. For group messaging, MLS (RFC 9420) has an Internet-Draft, draft-ietf-mls-pq-ciphersuites-06 (July 2026), that registers ML-KEM and PQ/T hybrid cipher suites.
main_source: Signal Protocol and Post-Quantum Ratchets

use_case_label: Algorand Falcon signatures (state proofs & logic-signature accounts)
summary: Per Algorand's own posts, its state proofs use Falcon-1024 signatures (State Proofs deployed in 2022), and a technical brief dated November 3, 2025 reports its first mainnet transaction using Falcon signatures, authorized through a logic signature that verifies them; the brief calls Falcon still experimental for securing accounts and the consensus layer. A roadmap dated June 18, 2026 and written by the Algorand Foundation says native post-quantum accounts will be introduced in the Q3 2026 protocol release; a footnote on the same page states they are live on mainnet as of August 2026, while the body of the page still says 'will be introduced'. Consensus messages are still signed with Ed25519, with research ongoing. These are Algorand's own statements, not an independent audit.
main_source: Algorand Post-Quantum Cryptography Roadmap
no_protocol_reason: Algorand's account and state-proof signing is a chain-specific mechanism, not a standardised network protocol tracked by the matrix.

use_case_label: Payments quantum-safe readiness roadmap (Nacha Payments Innovation Alliance)
summary: A strategic multi-year plan from Nacha's Payments Innovation Alliance quantum payments project team for transitioning to quantum-safe cryptographic solutions, in three phases: Now (years 1-2, mobilization and discovery), Next (years 2-4, planning and piloting) and Later (years 4+, migration and scaling). It calls for a cryptographic inventory and risk assessment and hybrid cryptography pilots, and says all requests for information and proposals should require vendors be quantum-safe by 2030.
main_source: Quantum-Safe Payments Readiness Implementation Road Map
no_protocol_reason: A payments readiness roadmap is organisation-level planning, not a standardised network protocol tracked by the matrix.

use_case_label: Clinician identity & healthcare PKI smart cards (HPKI)
summary: TOPPAN Digital, NICT and ISARA tested a smart card system whose hybrid certificates support both ML-DSA and ECDSA: TOPPAN Digital developed the hybrid-certificate support for the cards, ISARA the hybrid-certificate issuance for the private certificate authority and the ML-DSA firmware, and NICT the overall framework of H-LINCOS, the healthcare data system used for the test. From April to September 2024, cards supporting only current public-key cryptography and hybrid cards were used as HPKI (healthcare public key infrastructure) cards, the accreditation carried by healthcare professionals, and the release reports that ID authentication and browsing of the electronic health record system worked with either card type. This is a vendor-reported pilot on a NICT-operated testbed; TOPPAN Digital says it is planning limited practical implementations in 2025 and is targeting full-scale deployment in 2030.
main_source: TOPPAN Digital, NICT, and ISARA Develop Smart Card System Employing Hybrid Methodology to Support Post-Quantum Cryptography and Current Public-key Cryptography
no_protocol_reason: The source describes hybrid certificates on smart cards used for user authentication to a health-record system; it does not name a network protocol tracked by the protocol matrix.

use_case_label: ICP-Brasil digital certificates and signature algorithms (DOC-ICP-01.01 v6.0)
summary: Instrução Normativa ITI nº 35, dated 30 January 2026, amends DOC-ICP-01.01, the ICP-Brasil document of cryptographic standards and algorithms, and approves its version 6.0. The amended entries add ML-DSA (FIPS 204) for certificate-authority key generation (ML-DSA-65 or 87) and for end-user keys (ML-DSA-44), and list ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024 for key-agreement schemes and ML-KEM-768 or 1024 for the safekeeping of the holder's private key and its backup. The instruction takes effect on publication and the RSA, elliptic-curve and EdDSA options stay in the amended entries; the text does not say whether any certificate has yet been issued with ML-DSA or ML-KEM.
main_source: Instrução Normativa ITI nº 35, de 30 de janeiro de 2026
no_protocol_reason: The source is a national instruction that lists permitted algorithms, key sizes and signature suites for certificates; it names no protocol tracked by the protocol matrix.

use_case_label: Regulator expectations: cryptography mapping and board plans (APRA)
summary: In a speech published on 24 June 2026, an APRA member said APRA wants to see its regulated entities at least starting to map where cryptography is relied upon across their systems, data and third-party providers, including long-lived data and critical infrastructure. APRA oversees general insurance and reinsurance companies, life insurance and private health insurers, among others. The speech says APRA intends to step up its supervisory engagement on this over the coming year and will want evidence that boards understand the risk and are advancing plans to meet the ASD's recommended timeline: a plan to transition to post-quantum cryptography by the end of 2026 and a transition commenced by the end of 2028. These are expectations stated in a speech, not a rule, and the speech names no algorithm.
main_source: APRA Member Therese McCarthy Hockey's remarks to the 2026 AFIA Risk Summit, "Fighting fire with fire"
no_protocol_reason: A supervisory expectation about mapping cryptography and board oversight, not a protocol tracked by the Algorithms > Protocol Support matrix.

use_case_label: ePassports and machine-readable travel documents (eMRTD, ICAO Doc 9303)
summary: ICAO Doc 9303 specifies the chip security of ePassports: Passive Authentication verifies the issuing State's signature over the Document Security Object through Document Signer and Country Signing CA certificates, which participating States publish through the ICAO Public Key Directory; PACE guards against skimming and eavesdropping, Active and Chip Authentication authenticate the chip, and Terminal Authentication controls access to sensitive biometrics. Parts 11 and 12 name RSA (RSASSA-PSS and PKCS#1 v1.5), DSA, ECDSA, DH/ECDH, AES and SHA-224 to SHA-512. ICAO's TAG/TRIP working paper for its November 2025 meeting states that final specifications for quantum-safe eMRTDs are not yet available and recommends a new work item for the Document Issuing PKI and Passive Authentication; its information paper compares ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, Falcon (FN-DSA), LMS and XMSS. In May 2026 ICAO stated that it is in the process of specifying post-quantum cryptography for inclusion in Doc 9303, and an ISO/IEC SC17/WG3 update to the ICAO Facilitation Conference gives 2027 as the target for specifications of PQC algorithms in X.509 certificates and CMS. ICAO's NTWG and ISO WG 3 have identified Passive Authentication as the protocol most vulnerable to quantum computing, and the same deck calls the threat to the ICAO PKI urgent given the 10-year validity of eMRTDs now being issued.
main_source: ICAO Doc 9303 Part 11 — Security Mechanisms for MRTDs

use_case_label: National eID cards and PIV smart-card credentials
summary: The BSI eIDAS token specification TR-03110 v2.21 (December 2016), whose examples include the German ID card, maps PACE, Terminal Authentication and Chip Authentication to ECDH, RSA and ECDSA. For US PIV cards, NIST SP 800-78-5 (July 2024) sets RSA, ECDSA and ECDH and states that post-quantum algorithms will be specified in a future revision; NIST's initial working drafts of 12 June 2026 identify the changes expected to be needed to use ML-DSA and ML-KEM with PIV, and an April 2026 draft Federal PKI profile specifies ML-DSA PIV authentication certificates for a test environment.
main_source: Advanced Security Mechanisms for Machine Readable Travel Documents and eIDAS Token - Part 3: Common Specifications (BSI TR-03110, v2.21)

summary: The EUDI Wallet is specified in the Architecture and Reference Framework: wallet units support ISO/IEC 18013-5 and SD-JWT VC attestations, with OpenID4VP for remote presentation and OpenID4VCI for issuance. Algorithm choices appear in those specifications: OpenID4VP names ECDSA with SHA-256, and RFC 9901 requires SHA-256 support. RFC 9901 leaves post-quantum JWS algorithms to the application 'when they are ready'; ETSI TS 119 312 V2.1.1 states that it is incomplete for the needs of the EUDI-Wallet and that an update is in preparation.
main_source: EUDI Wallet ARF v2.9.0

summary: ISO/IEC 18013-5 defines the mobile driving licence as an mdoc: CBOR data secured with COSE, which a reader checks through issuer data authentication, mdoc authentication of the holder's device and, where the mDL requires it, reader authentication. OpenID4VP and OpenID4VCI profile the format and, in their examples, use ECDSA with SHA-256 on a P-256 key for the issuer signature (issuerAuth), and ECDSA on P-256 or HMAC 256/256 over an ECDH-derived key for the device. The cited documents describe no post-quantum profile.
main_source: OpenID for Verifiable Presentations 1.0

summary: An IDEMIA research paper, written after NIST's July 2022 selection of a first set of post-quantum algorithms, builds post-quantum and hybrid versions of two EMV payment protocols on a banking smart-card (an Arm Cortex-M3 derivative with a basic "toy" application profile), using NTRU or Kyber512 as the key-encapsulation mechanism and Falcon or Dilithium in the certificates. It reports that Dilithium-5 data reached the application's maximum capacity and could not be loaded, that most of the transaction time is the transmission of the card certificate chain to the terminal, and that such products are possible but several issues remain. EMVCo's position statement (8 March 2024, published September 2024) names no post-quantum mechanism: it says its Security Working Group will monitor and support standards development of quantum resistant solutions, and the quantum threat is on current projections unlikely prior to 2040. Mastercard's white paper cites a Banque de France report estimating 4 to 6 times more chip RAM for post-quantum algorithms and calls combining chip cards and quantum resistance a work in progress.
main_source: Post-Quantum Protocols for Banking Applications
no_protocol_reason: EMV card-to-terminal transaction commands are an EMVCo card and terminal specification, not a protocol tracked by the Algorithms > Protocol Support matrix.

summary: TCG's TPM 2.0 Library Specification Version 185 (published 12 March 2026) introduced support for ML-DSA, HashML-DSA, ML-KEM and EdDSA; its algorithm table ties ML-KEM and ML-DSA to NIST FIPS 203 and 204, with ML-KEM-512, -768 and -1024 and ML-DSA-44, -65 and -87 as parameter sets. The PC Client Platform TPM Profile Version 1.07 (published 23 March 2026) makes ML-KEM (768 or 1024) and ML-DSA (65 or 87) support mandatory beside RSA 3072 and ECC, adds a buffer-chunking mechanism for the larger commands and responses anticipated with post-quantum algorithms, and requires a TPM that ships with EK certificates to carry RSA 3072 or ECC P-384 together with ML-KEM. The EK Credential Profile Version 2.7 (published 16 March 2026) defines ML-KEM (storage) and ML-DSA (signing) EK templates beside the RSA and ECC ones.
main_source: TCG PC Client Specific Platform TPM Profile for TPM 2.0, Version 1.07 (Published)

use_case_label: Common Criteria certification of security ICs and dedicated security components
summary: The NIAP collaborative Protection Profile for Dedicated Security Component, version 2.1 (17 November 2025), covers one or more hardware components with their controlling operating system or firmware, and its revision history lists post-quantum cryptography for the v2.1 final publication. The NIAP Protection Profile for General Purpose Computing Platforms, version 2.0, gives a TPM or other secure element as an example of an on-platform dedicated security component. The cPP's allowed choices for signature generation and verification include LMS, XMSS, ML-DSA and HashML-DSA beside RSA, ECDSA and EdDSA, and ML-KEM is among its allowed choices for key encapsulation. NIAP Technical Decision TD1011 (26 March 2026) states that, to be listed on the NIAP product compliant list, each applicable cryptographic requirement must include at least one selection conforming to CNSA suite 1.0 or 2.0. NIAP Policy Letter #33 (31 August 2026) states that products not meeting CNSA 2.0 requirements for every cryptographic function will not be accepted into NIAP evaluation from 1 January 2028. The Security IC Platform Protection Profile, version 2.0 (16 December 2025), is a separate profile for security ICs.
main_source: NIAP collaborative Protection Profile for Dedicated Security Component, Version 2.1
no_protocol_reason: A Common Criteria evaluation profile for embedded security hardware and firmware (cryptographic operations, key storage, root of trust), not a network protocol tracked by the Algorithms > Protocol Support matrix.

use_case_label: eUICC chips (embedded SIM) and their certification
summary: GSMA's eUICC protection profile (SGP.25 v2.1, 3 February 2025; registered as BSI-CC-PP-0100) sets the assurance level at Common Criteria EAL4 augmented with ALC_DVS.2 and AVA_VAN.5 and names ECDSA signature verification, elliptic-curve key agreement (ECKA) and AES. Neither the profile, GSMA SGP.24 v2.4.4 nor ENISA's EUCC specification for eUICC names a post-quantum mechanism. SGP.24 says the IC/hardware platform on which the eUICC is based 'shall be certified to either PP-0084 or PP-0035'; ENISA's specification (version 1.0, public consultation, June 2024) calls certification voluntary and sets EAL4 augmented where an eUICC is certified. GSMA PQ.03 v2.0 says all migration strategies will require post-quantum cryptography on eUICCs at some point, and PQ.04 v1.0 (25 November 2024) says the GSMA eSIM group is actively working on a PQC version of RSP.
main_source: BSI-CC-PP-0100-V2-2025 — eUICC for Consumer and IoT Devices Protection Profile (GSMA SGP.25 v2.1)
no_protocol_reason: The eUICC chip is certified against a protection profile and provisioned over the GSMA RSP interfaces (SGP.22 and SGP.32), which the Algorithms > Protocol Support matrix does not track; the profile lists TLS 1.2 or later among the eUICC interfaces but names no target protocol.
common_criteria_profile: IC/hardware platform: BSI-CC-PP-0084 or BSI-CC-PP-0035; eUICC: GSMA SGP.25 = BSI-CC-PP-0100-V2-2025 (EAL4 augmented with ALC_DVS.2 and AVA_VAN.5)

On its product page it says the SLC27 security controller (TEGRION family) is Common Criteria EAL6+ certified and includes a cryptographic library with ML-KEM and ML-DSA, and that in January 2025 it received the first Common Criteria EAL6+ certificate for a security controller comprising a post-quantum algorithm (ML-KEM). It also says two OPTIGA TPMs use XMSS for firmware updates, a PSoC microcontroller line supports LMS/XMSS firmware protection with a roadmap toward ML-DSA and ML-KEM, and a further TPM will be coming in 2027.
